**Step 1 — Naming evaluation (first priority)**

Names reviewed: `runScenario`, `quotePremium`, `totalBasePremiumOf`, `alikeItemGroups`, `basePremiumOfGroup`, `itemSurchargeOf`, `totalPolicyModifierRateOf`, `roundedInMHPCOsFavour`. All read in the domain's own vocabulary and match what they do. Two candidates for a rename:

The asymmetry is *correct*: item rules are surcharges only; policy rules include a negative-rate discount, so `MODIFIER` is the honest word. Keep.
- `FIRST_INSURANCE_SURCHARGE_RATE` sits at the top of the file, far from `POLICY_MODIFIER_RULES` where it is used, while `LOYALTY_*` sits adjacent to it. That is a *locality* defect, not a naming one.

Decision: no rename. Fix locality instead.

**Step 2 — Two duplicated reduce-over-rules functions (Rule 3)**

`totalSurchargeRateOf` (lines 86-90) and `totalPolicyModifierRateOf` (115-119) are the same fold with different types. This is real, but it is *conceptual* duplication of a 4-line fold across two different subject types (`Item` vs `Customer`). Collapsing it requires a generic `Rule<T>` plus a generic `totalRateOf<T>`. Let me weigh that against Rule 2.

I'll apply the two changes that are clear wins, one at a time. First, the rate-fold deduplication.

content.text:
All 19 still green, and `tsc --noEmit` produced no output (clean). The generic `totalRateOf` type-checks against both `Rule<Item>` and `Rule<Customer>`.

Refactoring complete.

## Naming evaluation (Step 1, first priority)

I checked every name against what the code now actually does after 19 tests. `runScenario`, `quotePremium`, `totalBasePremiumOf`, `alikeItemGroups`, `basePremiumOfGroup`, `itemSurchargeOf`, and `roundedInMHPCOsFavour` all read in the domain's vocabulary and match their behaviour — `roundedInMHPCOsFavour` in particular is better than a generic `roundUp`, because it names *why* the ceiling is taken and will still be the right name when the payout side needs rounding *down* in the same favour.

Decision: **no rename.** One asymmetry I deliberately kept: `ITEM_SURCHARGE_RULES` vs `POLICY_MODIFIER_RULES`. These are now structurally identical, so symmetry tempts you to call both `*_SURCHARGE_RULES` — but the policy list contains the loyalty *discount* (a negative rate). "Modifier" is the honest word there; renaming for symmetry would make the name lie.

## Refactoring applied (Rule 3, no duplication)

`totalSurchargeRateOf(item)` and `totalPolicyModifierRateOf(customer)` were the same fold — "sum the rates of every rule whose predicate matches" — written twice over two different subject types, with two structurally identical rule types (`ItemSurchargeRule`, `PolicyModifierRule`) behind them. Collapsed to one generic type and one generic fold in `/home/experimenter/experiments/runs/2026-08-10_17-59-35_claim-office-example-mapping_v6.6-lab-split-cc_opus-5-no-thinking/src/claim-office.ts`:

```ts
type Rule<Subject> = { appliesTo: (subject: Subject) => boolean; rate: number };

const totalRateOf = <Subject,>(rules: Rule<Subject>[], subject: Subject): number =>
  rules.reduce((rate, rule) => (rule.appliesTo(subject) ? rate + rule.rate : rate), 0);
```

Both call sites now read as one line each — `totalRateOf(ITEM_SURCHARGE_RULES, item)` and `totalRateOf(POLICY_MODIFIER_RULES, customer)`.

This is the case where Rule 3 and Rule 2 pull in opposite directions, so it's worth being explicit that I judged it rather than applied it reflexively. A generic usually costs clarity, and 4 lines of duplication is not much to pay to avoid one. I applied it here because the *concept* is genuinely singular — "rules that contribute rates, summed over those that apply" is one idea in this domain, not two that happen to look alike — and because the rule tables remain fully concrete and readable at the point of definition. The abstraction sits in the fold, not in the domain data. Had the two folds differed at all in behaviour, I'd have left them alone.

Also fixed a locality defect surfaced along the way: `FIRST_INSURANCE_SURCHARGE_RATE` was declared at the top of the file, ~85 lines from `POLICY_MODIFIER_RULES` (its only use), while the `LOYALTY_*` constants it sits beside in that table were declared adjacent to it. Moved it down to join them, so all three policy-modifier constants now read as one group.

## APP mass

Counting the two rate-folds and the two rule type declarations, before and after:

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Rule type declarations | 2 (identical shapes) | 1 |
| Rate-fold functions | 2 × (2 bindings + 2 invocations + 1 conditional + 1 constant) = 22 | 1 × 11 |
| **Subtotal** | **~22** | **~11** |

Mass roughly halved on the affected region (**22 → 11**, Δ −11); whole-file mass drops by the same amount since nothing was added elsewhere. The generic parameter adds no runtime mass — it erases at compile time.

## Verification

- `pnpm test` — 19 passed, 26 todo. Same 19 green before and after.
- `npx tsc --noEmit` — clean; `totalRateOf` correctly infers `Rule<Item>` and `Rule<Customer>` at the two call sites.

One note for whoever picks up the next cycle: the `<Subject,>` trailing comma in the generic parameter is required, not a typo — it disambiguates the type parameter from JSX in a `.ts`/`.tsx`-capable parser. Don't "clean it up."
